lesson.title: Cube Roots: The Root That Handles Negative Numbers Too
lesson.summary: A cube root asks what number, cubed, gives back the value inside the radical, and unlike square roots, cube roots are perfectly comfortable with negative numbers.
lesson.body:
Just as a square root undoes squaring, a cube root undoes raising a number to the power of 3. The cube root of a number b, written with a small 3 in the crook of the radical symbol as the cube root of b, is the number that produces b when cubed. For example, the cube root of 125 is 5, because 5^3 = 5 times 5 times 5 = 125.

Recognizing perfect cubes speeds this up the same way recognizing perfect squares helped with square roots. The first several perfect cubes are 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, and 216, coming from cubing 1 through 6. Once these are familiar, the cube root of 64 is immediately 4, since 4^3 = 64, with no guessing required.

The most important difference between cube roots and square roots involves negative numbers, and it comes directly from how signs behave under multiplication. Squaring a negative number always gives a positive result, because a negative times a negative is positive, which is why no real number squares to a negative value. Cubing works differently: a negative number times itself three times stays negative, because you multiply an even number of negatives (giving positive) and then one more negative, flipping the sign back. So the cube root of -27 is -3, because (-3)^3 = (-3) times (-3) times (-3) = 9 times (-3) = -27. This means, unlike square roots, cube roots are always defined for negative inputs, and every real number, positive, negative, or zero, has exactly one real cube root.

Cube roots apply to algebraic expressions the same way they apply to plain numbers, as long as you track the exponent on each factor correctly. To simplify the cube root of 8x^3, look for a quantity that, when cubed, reproduces 8x^3. Since 2^3 = 8 and (x)^3 = x^3, cubing 2x gives (2x)^3 = 2^3 times x^3 = 8x^3, exactly the expression under the radical. So the cube root of 8x^3 equals 2x.

Cube roots and square roots are both special cases of a more general idea, the nth root, where the small number tucked into the radical (called the index) tells you what power to undo. A square root is really just an index-2 root with the 2 left off by convention, and a cube root is an index-3 root. Keeping the square root lesson in mind while learning cube roots helps highlight exactly where the two behave the same, such as recognizing perfect powers, and exactly where they part ways, such as how they treat negative numbers.

Another useful check is to confirm that cubing and cube-rooting really do undo each other in both directions, the same round-trip test used for square roots. Start with -4, cube it to get (-4)^3 = -64, and the cube root of -64 should return -4. Checking, the cube root of -64 does equal -4, since (-4)^3 = (-4) times (-4) times (-4) = 16 times (-4) = -64, confirming the round trip. This is why the cube root is described as the inverse operation of cubing, in the same sense that the square root is the inverse of squaring, but with the extra flexibility of handling every real number, not just the nonnegative ones. A second numeric example reinforces the sign rule with a slightly larger perfect cube. Evaluate the cube root of -216. Since 6^3 = 216, and cubing a negative number keeps the result negative, (-6)^3 = -216. So the cube root of -216 is -6. There is no ambiguity here about a principal root the way there was with square roots, since a real number has only one real cube root, whether the number is positive, negative, or zero, which makes cube roots slightly simpler to work with once the sign behavior is understood.
